actions.justification: Mandatory first-step action. Patient presents with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum with known COPD and pneumothorax — respiratory status assessment is critical to characterize severity of this likely COPD exacerbation.
Mandatory action. Full vital sign assessment is required as the initial step in evaluating any acute presentation, particularly with dyspnea in a COPD patient.
Mandatory action. Chest X-ray is essential to evaluate for pneumothorax (given history), consolidation, hyperinflation, or other causes of acute dyspnea in this COPD patient.
MANDATORY: ABG is essential in AECOPD to assess PaO2, PaCO2, and pH, identifying hypercapnic respiratory failure and guiding oxygen therapy and NIV decisions.
Mental status assessment is critical in COPD exacerbation to detect hypercapnic encephalopathy (confusion, somnolence), which would indicate urgent NIV or intubation need.
Short-acting bronchodilators (SABA/SAMA) are first-line treatment for AECOPD to relieve bronchospasm and improve airflow.
Patient has COPD with worsening dyspnea; supplemental oxygen should be provided carefully (targeting SpO2 88-92% in COPD) to correct any underlying hypoxemia, though current SpO2 is 98%.
COPD exacerbation with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production; systemic corticosteroids are a guideline-recommended treatment to reduce inflammation and shorten exacerbation duration.
Patient has COPD exacerbation with history of pneumothorax; pulmonology consult is warranted for complex management decisions and to guide further workup and treatment.
CBC is essential to evaluate for leukocytosis suggesting bacterial infection driving this COPD exacerbation with increased sputum production. Will guide antibiotic decision-making.
BMP to assess electrolytes, renal function, and glucose - important baseline in COPD exacerbation, especially if steroids are being administered, and to guide further management.

Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) is a key intervention in COPD exacerbations. Assessing NIV eligibility now is critical - especially given prior pneumothorax history which may be a contraindication, and current respiratory symptoms.

Patient presents with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum production consistent with COPD exacerbation, likely infectious etiology. Sputum culture will identify causative organism to guide antibiotic therapy.
Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral COPD exacerbation, guiding antibiotic stewardship in this patient with increased sputum production.

Patient has known history of pneumothorax as a comorbidity. CT chest provides detailed assessment of lung parenchyma, can identify recurrent pneumothorax, bullous disease, or other structural changes contributing to dyspnea beyond what chest X-ray reveals.
AECOPD with increased purulent sputum raises concern for bacterial infection/sepsis. Blood cultures should be obtained before initiating antibiotics to identify causative organisms.
Lactate helps assess for occult tissue hypoperfusion or early sepsis in the context of AECOPD with infectious symptoms, even though the patient appears hemodynamically stable.

GOLD guidelines recommend antibiotics for AECOPD with increased purulent sputum (Anthonisen Type 1 exacerbation). Blood cultures ordered first; antibiotics indicated now to treat likely bacterial exacerbation.

Patient with COPD exacerbation and worsening dyspnea may benefit from cautious IV fluid administration to maintain hydration, especially if sputum production is increased and patient may be dehydrated. Vitals are stable (BP 120/80, HR 80, SpO2 98%) allowing for careful fluid resuscitation while monitoring for fluid overload.

Patient with COPD and history of pneumothorax presenting with worsening dyspnea. While primary workup and treatment are underway, a diuretic may help if there is any fluid overload component contributing to dyspnea. SpO2 is 98% and vitals are stable, but diuretic can be considered cautiously to reduce any pulmonary congestion. This is an optional action available in the current phase.

Patient has COPD exacerbation with worsening dyspnea. While vitals are currently stable (BP 120/80, MAP 103), this is the only available action remaining in the current phase. Vasopressor use should be cautious given stable hemodynamics, but it is the sole available action to select from the provided list.
Multiple labs are pending (CBC, BMP, ABG, sputum culture, procalcitonin, lactate). Reviewing results will guide further management decisions including antibiotic selection and ventilatory support.
Continuous monitoring of SpO2 is essential in COPD exacerbation to ensure target saturation (88-92%) is maintained without oxygen-induced hypercapnia.
CBC, BMP, ABG, procalcitonin, and sputum culture results are pending; reviewing these will guide antibiotic selection, assess severity of exacerbation, and inform further management decisions.
